explanatories.IsPrimitiveRoot.isIntegral: A primitive root of unity is an integral element over the integers.
explanatories.Algebra.IsIntegral.isIntegral: If an algebra over a commutative ring is integral, then every element of that algebra is also integral over the commutative ring.
explanatories.Subalgebra.sub_mem: The difference between any two elements in a subalgebra remains within that subalgebra.
explanatories.Algebra.self_mem_adjoin_singleton: The theorem asserts that any element is contained within the subalgebra generated by itself.
explanatories.Subalgebra.one_mem: The unity element is included in every subalgebra of a given algebraic structure.
explanatories.IsPrimitiveRoot.integralPowerBasis: The integral power basis of the ring of integers in a cyclotomic extension given a primitive root of unity is established for that extension.
explanatories.IsPrimitiveRoot.toInteger: This definition provides a way to interpret a primitive root of unity as an element of the ring of integers in the context of a field.
explanatories.IsPrimitiveRoot.integralPowerBasis_gen: The generator of the integral power basis associated with a primitive root of unity in a cyclotomic extension is equal to its corresponding integer representation.
explanatories.PowerBasis.ofGenMemAdjoin': The power basis for an algebra can be constructed from an integral element if its generator is an element of the algebra generated by adjoining that integral element.
explanatories.NumberField.RingOfIntegers.isIntegral: This theorem states that any element from the ring of integers of a number field is integral over the integers.
explanatories.Subalgebra.add_mem: The sum of two elements in a subalgebra is also an element of that subalgebra.
explanatories.Subsemiring.coe_add: This theorem states that the addition of two elements from a subsemiring, when viewed in the context of the larger semiring, is equal to the image of their sum in the subsemiring.
explanatories.Subalgebra.coe_toSubsemiring: The natural representation of a subalgebra as a subsemiring is equivalent to its original form in the context of basic algebraic structure.
explanatories.OneMemClass.coe_one: The identity element in a structure that follows the OneMemClass property is represented as one.
explanatories.sub_add_cancel: In an additive group, subtracting an element from another and then adding the subtracted element back yields the original element.
explanatories.Finsupp.coe_add: This theorem states that the function corresponding to the sum of two finitely supported functions is equal to the sum of the functions corresponding to each individual finitely supported function.

IsPrimitiveRoot.subOneIntegralPowerBasis.description: The element formed by subtracting one from a primitive root of unity in a cyclotomic extension provides an integral basis for that extension.

IsCyclotomicExtension.Rat.absdiscr_prime.code:
IsCyclotomicExtension.Rat.absdiscr_prime_pow.{u} (p : ℕ+) (k : ℕ) (K : Type u) [Field K] [CharZero K]
  [hp : Fact (Nat.Prime ↑p)] [IsCyclotomicExtension {p ^ k} ℚ K] :
  NumberField.discr K = (-1) ^ (φ (↑p ^ k) / 2) * ↑↑p ^ (↑p ^ (k - 1) * ((↑p - 1) * k - 1))
IsCyclotomicExtension.Rat.absdiscr_prime.comment:
We compute the absolute discriminant of a `p ^ k`-th cyclotomic field.
Beware that in the cases `p ^ k = 1` and `p ^ k = 2` the formula uses `1 / 2 = 0` and `0 - 1 = 0`.
See also the results below.

EisensteinSeries.summand_bound.comment:
Upper bound for the summand `|c * z + d| ^ (-k)`, as a product of a function of `z` and a
function of `c, d`.

EisensteinSeries.summand_bound.description: This theorem provides an upper bound for a summand involving the absolute value of a linear combination of a complex variable and integer components, demonstrating that it can be expressed as a product of a function related to the complex variable and the norm of the integer components raised to a negative power.

EisensteinSeries.eisensteinSeries_tendst.code:
EisensteinSeries.eisensteinSeries_tendstoLocallyUniformly {k : ℤ} (hk : 3 ≤ k) {N : ℕ} (a : Fin 2 → ZMod N) :
  TendstoLocallyUniformly (fun s x => ∑ x_1 ∈ s, eisSummand k (↑x_1) x) (fun x => eisensteinSeries a k x) Filter.atTop
EisensteinSeries.eisensteinSeries_tendst.comment:
The sum defining the Eisenstein series (of weight `k` and level `Γ(N)` with congruence
condition `a : Fin 2 → ZMod N`) converges locally uniformly on `ℍ`.

explanatories.ZMod: This definition introduces the type representing integers under modulo operation for a given natural number.
explanatories.TendstoLocallyUniformly: A sequence of functions converges locally uniformly to a limiting function with respect to a filter if, for any entourage of the diagonal and for any point, the function values in a neighborhood of that point become arbitrarily close as determined by the filter.
explanatories.EisensteinSeries.eisSummand: This definition describes a function that, given an integer, a pair of integers, and a complex variable, produces a complex number contributing to the sum that defines an Eisenstein series.
explanatories.Filter.atTop: This definition introduces a filter that captures the behavior of elements approaching infinity in an ordered set, generated by all sets containing elements greater than or equal to any given element.

EisensteinSeries.eisensteinSeries_tendst.description: This theorem asserts that the sum defining the Eisenstein series for a given weight and level converges locally uniformly on the upper half-plane.

EisensteinSeries.summable_norm_eisSumman.code: EisensteinSeries.summable_norm_eisSummand {k : ℤ} (hk : 3 ≤ k) (z : ℍ) : Summable fun x => ‖eisSummand k x z‖

explanatories.Summable: A function is considered summable if it possesses a defined infinite sum, which can be computed using the specified summation operator.

EisensteinSeries.summable_norm_eisSumman.description: This theorem asserts that for integer values greater than or equal to three, the norms of the summands in the Eisenstein series are summable for elements in the upper half-plane.

EisensteinSeries.abs_le_tsum_abs.code:
EisensteinSeries.abs_le_tsum_abs (N : ℕ) (a : Fin 2 → ZMod N) (k : ℤ) (hk : 3 ≤ k) (z : ℍ) :
  Complex.abs (eisensteinSeries a k z) ≤ ∑' (x : Fin 2 → ℤ), Complex.abs (eisSummand k x z)
EisensteinSeries.abs_le_tsum_abs.comment: The absolute value of the restricted sum is less than the full sum of the absolute values.

explanatories.Complex.abs: The definition specifies a function that calculates the absolute value of a complex number as the square root of its norm squared.
explanatories.ZMod: This definition introduces the type representing integers under modulo operation for a given natural number.

EisensteinSeries.abs_le_tsum_abs.description: This theorem establishes that the absolute value of the Eisenstein series associated with a given sequence is bounded above by the sum of the absolute values of its corresponding summands.

EisensteinSeries.div_linear_zpow_differe.code:
EisensteinSeries.div_linear_zpow_differentiableOn (k : ℤ) (a : Fin 2 → ℤ) :
  DifferentiableOn ℂ (fun z => (↑(a 0) * z + ↑(a 1)) ^ (-k)) {z | 0 < z.im}
EisensteinSeries.div_linear_zpow_differe.comment:
Auxilary lemma showing that for any `k : ℤ` the function `z → 1/(c*z+d)^k` is
differentiable on `{z : ℂ | 0 < z.im}`.

explanatories.DifferentiableOn: A function is differentiable on a set if it is differentiable at every point within that set.

EisensteinSeries.div_linear_zpow_differe.description: This theorem demonstrates that the function which inverts a linear combination of a complex variable is differentiable in regions where the imaginary part of the variable is positive.

EisensteinSeries.eisSummand_extension_di.code:
EisensteinSeries.eisSummand_extension_differentiableOn (k : ℤ) (a : Fin 2 → ℤ) :
  DifferentiableOn ℂ (eisSummand k a ∘ ↑ofComplex) {z | 0 < z.im}
EisensteinSeries.eisSummand_extension_di.comment:
Auxilary lemma showing that for any `k : ℤ` and `(a : Fin 2 → ℤ)`
the extension of `eisSummand` is differentiable on `{z : ℂ | 0 < z.im}`.

explanatories.DifferentiableOn: A function is differentiable on a set if it is differentiable at every point within that set.

EisensteinSeries.eisSummand_extension_di.description: This theorem establishes that the extension of a specific mathematical function is differentiable in areas where the imaginary part of the complex variable is greater than zero.

sum_range_pow.code:
sum_range_pow (n p : ℕ) :
  ∑ k ∈ range n, ↑k ^ p = ∑ i ∈ range (p + 1), bernoulli i * ↑((p + 1).choose i) * ↑n ^ (p + 1 - i) / (↑p + 1)
sum_range_pow.comment:
**Faulhaber's theorem** relating the **sum of p-th powers** to the Bernoulli numbers:
$$\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k^p = \sum_{i=0}^p B_i\binom{p+1}{i}\frac{n^{p+1-i}}{p+1}.$$
See https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Faulhaber%27s_Formula and [orosi2018faulhaber] for
the proof provided here.

EulerProduct.eulerProduct_hasProd.code:
EulerProduct.eulerProduct_hasProd.{u_1} {R : Type u_1} [NormedCommRing R] [CompleteSpace R] {f : ℕ → R} (hf₁ : f 1 = 1)
  (hmul : ∀ {m n : ℕ}, m.Coprime n → f (m * n) = f m * f n) (hsum : Summable fun x => ‖f x‖) (hf₀ : f 0 = 0) :
  HasProd (fun p => ∑' (e : ℕ), f (↑p ^ e)) (∑' (n : ℕ), f n)
EulerProduct.eulerProduct_hasProd.comment:
The *Euler Product* for multiplicative (on coprime arguments) functions.

If `f : ℕ → R`, where `R` is a complete normed commutative ring, `f 0 = 0`, `f 1 = 1`, `f` is
multiplicative on coprime arguments, and `‖f ·‖` is summable, then
`∏' p : Nat.Primes, ∑' e, f (p ^ e) = ∑' n, f n`. This version is stated using `HasProd`.

explanatories.Summable: A function is considered summable if it possesses a defined infinite sum, which can be computed using the specified summation operator.
explanatories.HasProd: An infinite product on a topological monoid is defined as the limit of products over increasingly larger finite subsets, and this product operation is also robust against reordering of terms.

EulerProduct.eulerProduct_hasProd.description: This theorem asserts that if a function defined on natural numbers is multiplicative with specific properties, including summability and a defined value at zero, then the infinite sum over all natural numbers equals the product of sums over its prime factorization.

EulerProduct.eulerProduct_hasProd_mulInd.comment:

If `f : ℕ → R`, where `R` is a complete normed commutative ring, `f 0 = 0`, `f 1 = 1`, `f` i
multiplicative on coprime arguments, and `‖f ·‖` is summable, then
`∏' p : ℕ, if p.Prime then ∑' e, f (p ^ e) else 1 = ∑' n, f n`.
This version is stated using `HasProd` and `Set.mulIndicator`.

  Tendsto (fun n => ∏ p ∈ n.primesBelow, ∑' (e : ℕ), f (p ^ e)) atTop (𝓝 (∑' (n : ℕ), f n))
EulerProduct.eulerProduct.comment:
The *Euler Product* for multiplicative (on coprime arguments) functions.

If `f : ℕ → R`, where `R` is a complete normed commutative ring, `f 0 = 0`, `f 1 = 1`, `f` is
multiplicative on coprime arguments, and `‖f ·‖` is summable, then
`∏' p : {p : ℕ | p.Prime}, ∑' e, f (p ^ e) = ∑' n, f n`.
This is a version using convergence of finite partial products.

EulerProduct.summable_and_hasSum_factore.code:
EulerProduct.summable_and_hasSum_factoredNumbers_prod_filter_prime_geometric.{u_1} {F : Type u_1} [NormedField F]
  [CompleteSpace F] {f : ℕ →* F} (h : ∀ {p : ℕ}, Nat.Prime p → ‖f p‖ < 1) (s : Finset ℕ) :
  (Summable fun m => ‖f ↑m‖) ∧ HasSum (fun m => f ↑m) (∏ p ∈ filter Nat.Prime s, (1 - f p)⁻¹)
EulerProduct.summable_and_hasSum_factore.comment:
Given a (completely) multiplicative function `f : ℕ → F`, where `F` is a normed field,
such that `‖f p‖ < 1` for all primes `p`, we can express the sum of `f n` over all `s`-factored
positive integers `n` as a product of `(1 - f p)⁻¹` over the primes `p ∈ s`. At the same time,
we show that the sum involved converges absolutely.

EulerProduct.summable_and_hasSum_factore.description: This theorem demonstrates that for a completely multiplicative function defined on natural numbers that is bounded below one for all prime inputs, the infinite sum of the function over positive integers factored by a given set of primes converges absolutely and can be expressed as a product of specific inverses related to those primes.

riemannZetaSummandHom.fullDefinition: def riemannZetaSummandHom (hs : s ≠ 0) : ℕ →*₀ ℂ where   toFun n := (n : ℂ) ^ (-s)   map_zero' := by simp [hs]   map_one' := by simp   map_mul' m n := by     simpa only [Nat.cast_mul, ofReal_natCast]       using mul_cpow_ofReal_nonneg m.cast_nonneg n.cast_nonneg _
riemannZetaSummandHom.description: This definition specifies a completely multiplicative function that maps each natural number to its reciprocal raised to a non-zero complex power, and that function equals zero at zero.

dirichletSummandHom.fullDefinition: def dirichletSummandHom {n : ℕ} (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ n) (hs : s ≠ 0) : ℕ →*₀ ℂ where   toFun n := χ n * (n : ℂ) ^ (-s)   map_zero' := by simp [hs]   map_one' := by simp   map_mul' m n := by     simp_rw [← ofReal_natCast]     simpa only [Nat.cast_mul, IsUnit.mul_iff, not_and, map_mul, ofReal_mul,       mul_cpow_ofReal_nonneg m.cast_nonneg n.cast_nonneg _]       using mul_mul_mul_comm ..
dirichletSummandHom.description: This definition describes a completely multiplicative function that maps each natural number to the product of a Dirichlet character and its reciprocal raised to a non-zero complex power, while equating to zero at zero.

tsum_riemannZetaSummand.code: tsum_riemannZetaSummand {s : ℂ} (hs : 1 < s.re) : ∑' (n : ℕ), (riemannZetaSummandHom ⋯) n = riemannZeta s

ModularGroup.lcRow0Extend_apply.code:
ModularGroup.lcRow0Extend_apply {cd : Fin 2 → ℤ} (hcd : IsCoprime (cd 0) (cd 1))
  (f : (i : Fin 2) → (fun a => Fin 2 → ℝ) i) (i : Fin 2) :
  ∀ (a : Fin 2),
    (lcRow0Extend hcd) f i a =
      (![(LinearMap.GeneralLinearGroup.generalLinearEquiv ℝ (Fin 2 → ℝ))

ModularGroup.smul_eq_lcRow0_add.code:
ModularGroup.smul_eq_lcRow0_add {g : SL(2, ℤ)} (z : ℍ) {p : Fin 2 → ℤ} (hp : IsCoprime (p 0) (p 1)) (hg : ↑g 1 = p) :
  ↑(g • z) =
    ↑((lcRow0 p) ↑((SpecialLinearGroup.map (Int.castRingHom ℝ)) g)) / (↑(p 0) ^ 2 + ↑(p 1) ^ 2) +
      (↑(p 1) * ↑z - ↑(p 0)) / ((↑(p 0) ^ 2 + ↑(p 1) ^ 2) * (↑(p 0) * ↑z + ↑(p 1)))
ModularGroup.smul_eq_lcRow0_add.comment:
This replaces `(g•z).re = a/c + *` in the standard theory with the following novel identity:
`g • z = (a c + b d) / (c^2 + d^2) + (d z - c) / ((c^2 + d^2) (c z + d))`
which does not need to be decomposed depending on whether `c = 0`.

ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt.comment:
The `vonMangoldt` function is the function on natural numbers that returns `log p` if the input can
be expressed as `p^k` for a prime `p`.
In the case when `n` is a prime power, `min_fac` will give the appropriate prime, as it is the
smallest prime factor.

In the `ArithmeticFunction` locale, we have the notation `Λ` for this function.
This is also available in the `ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt` locale, allowing for selective
access to the notation.

explanatories.Real.log: The real logarithm function is defined to extend the conventional logarithm to all real numbers, assigning specific values for positive, negative, and zero inputs while preserving key logarithmic properties.
explanatories.ArithmeticFunction.log: The logarithm is defined as a specific type of arithmetic function that maps natural numbers to real numbers.
explanatories.IsPrimePow: A number is defined as a prime power if it can be expressed as a prime raised to a positive integer exponent.
explanatories.if_neg: If a condition is proven to be false, then the result of a conditional expression will yield the alternative value.
explanatories.not_isPrimePow_zero: Zero is not a prime power.

ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt.fullDefinition: noncomputable def vonMangoldt : ArithmeticFunction ℝ :=   ⟨fun n => if IsPrimePow n then Real.log (minFac n) else 0, if_neg not_isPrimePow_zero⟩
ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt.description: The von Mangoldt function is defined as an arithmetic function that assigns the logarithm of a prime to natural numbers that can be represented as prime powers.

be expressed as `p^k` for a prime `p`.
In the case when `n` is a prime power, `min_fac` will give the appropriate prime, as it is the
smallest prime factor.

In the `ArithmeticFunction` locale, we have the notation `Λ` for this function.
This is also available in the `ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt` locale, allowing for selective
access to the notation.

Real.exists_int_int_abs_mul_sub_le.code:
Real.exists_int_int_abs_mul_sub_le (ξ : ℝ) {n : ℕ} (n_pos : 0 < n) :
  ∃ j k, 0 < k ∧ k ≤ ↑n ∧ |↑k * ξ - ↑j| ≤ 1 / (↑n + 1)
Real.exists_int_int_abs_mul_sub_le.comment:
*Dirichlet's approximation theorem:*
For any real number `ξ` and positive natural `n`, there are integers `j` and `k`,
with `0 < k ≤ n` and `|k*ξ - j| ≤ 1/(n+1)`.

See also `Real.exists_nat_abs_mul_sub_round_le`.
Real.exists_int_int_abs_mul_sub_le.description: For any real number and a positive natural number, there exist integers that fulfill specific bounds on their product and difference.

Real.convergent.comment:
We give a direct recursive definition of the convergents of the continued fraction
expansion of a real number `ξ`. The main reason for that is that we want to have the
convergents as rational numbers; the versions `(GenContFract.of ξ).convs` and
`(GenContFract.of ξ).convs'` always give something of the same type as `ξ`.
We can then also use dot notation `ξ.convergent n`.
Another minor reason is that this demonstrates that the proof
of Legendre's theorem does not need anything beyond this definition.
We provide a proof that this definition agrees with the other one;
see `Real.convs_eq_convergent`.
(Note that we use the fact that `1/0 = 0` here to make it work for rational `ξ`.)
Real.convergent.fullDefinition: noncomputable def convergent : ℝ → ℕ → ℚ   | ξ, 0 => ⌊ξ⌋   | ξ, n + 1 => ⌊ξ⌋ + (convergent (fract ξ)⁻¹ n)⁻¹
Real.convergent.description: The convergents of a real number's continued fraction expansion are defined as a sequence of rational numbers generated recursively from that real number.

We can then also use dot notation `ξ.convergent n`.
Another minor reason is that this demonstrates that the proof

We provide a proof that this definition agrees with the other one;

euler_four_squares.code:
_root_.euler_four_squares.{u_1} {R : Type u_1} [CommRing R] (a b c d x y z w : R) :
  (a * x - b * y - c * z - d * w) ^ 2 + (a * y + b * x + c * w - d * z) ^ 2 + (a * z - b * w + c * x + d * y) ^ 2 +
      (a * w + b * z - c * y + d * x) ^ 2 =
    (a ^ 2 + b ^ 2 + c ^ 2 + d ^ 2) * (x ^ 2 + y ^ 2 + z ^ 2 + w ^ 2)
euler_four_squares.description: The theorem demonstrates that the sum of the squares of four specific polynomial expressions equals the product of the sum of the squares of the coefficients and the sum of the squares of four variables, which reflects Euler's four-square identity.

Int.sq_add_sq_of_two_mul_sq_add_sq.description: The theorem establishes a relationship that allows expressing an integer as the sum of two squares derived from another integer's squared components, specifically when that integer is half the sum of two squares.

`n` is a probable prime to base `b` if `n` passes the Fermat primality test; that is, `n` divides
`b ^ (n - 1) - 1`.

probable primes to any base.

_private.«.lake».packages.mathlib.Mathli.code: Nat.psp_from_prime (b p : ℕ) : ℕ
_private.«.lake».packages.mathlib.Mathli.comment:
Given a prime `p` which does not divide `b * (b ^ 2 - 1)`, we can produce a number `n` which is
larger than `p` and pseudoprime to base `b`. We do this by defining
`n = ((b ^ p - 1) / (b - 1)) * ((b ^ p + 1) / (b + 1))`

The primary purpose of this definition is to help prove `exists_infinite_pseudoprimes`. For a proof
that `n` is actually pseudoprime to base `b`, see `psp_from_prime_psp`, and for a proof that `n` is
greater than `p`, see `psp_from_prime_gt_p`.

This lemma is intended to be used when `2 ≤ b`, `2 < p`, `p` is prime, and `¬p ∣ b * (b ^ 2 - 1)`,
because those are the hypotheses for `psp_from_prime_psp`.
_private.«.lake».packages.mathlib.Mathli.fullDefinition: private def psp_from_prime (b : ℕ) (p : ℕ) : ℕ :=   (b ^ p - 1) / (b - 1) * ((b ^ p + 1) / (b + 1))
_private.«.lake».packages.mathlib.Mathli.description: This definition outlines a method to create a number that is greater than a given prime and acts as a pseudoprime with respect to a specified base, provided certain divisibility conditions are met.

  (P : Ideal S) : ℕ
Ideal.ramificationIdx.comment:
The ramification index of `P` over `p` is the largest exponent `n` such that
`p` is contained in `P^n`.

In particular, if `p` is not contained in `P^n`, then the ramification index is 0.

If there is no largest such `n` (e.g. because `p = ⊥`), then `ramificationIdx` is
defined to be 0.

  [p.IsMaximal] : ℕ
Ideal.inertiaDeg.comment:
The inertia degree of `P : Ideal S` lying over `p : Ideal R` is the degree of the
extension `(S / P) : (R / p)`.

We do not assume `P` lies over `p` in the definition; we return `0` instead.

See `inertiaDeg_algebraMap` for the common case where `f = algebraMap R S`
and there is an algebra structure `R / p → S / P`.

Ideal.inertiaDeg.fullDefinition: noncomputable def inertiaDeg [p.IsMaximal] : ℕ :=   if hPp : comap f P = p then     @finrank (R ⧸ p) (S ⧸ P) _ _ <|       @Algebra.toModule _ _ _ _ <|         RingHom.toAlgebra <|           Ideal.Quotient.lift p ((Ideal.Quotient.mk P).comp f) fun _ ha =>             Quotient.eq_zero_iff_mem.mpr <| mem_comap.mp <| hPp.symm ▸ ha   else 0
Ideal.inertiaDeg.description: The inertia degree of an ideal in one ring over an ideal in another ring is defined as the degree of the corresponding field extension, with a special case returning zero if the ideals are not properly related.

ideal.inertia_deg.code:
Ideal.inertiaDeg.{u, v} {R : Type u} [CommRing R] {S : Type v} [CommRing S] (f : R →+* S) (p : Ideal R) (P : Ideal S)
  [p.IsMaximal] : ℕ
ideal.inertia_deg.comment:
The inertia degree of `P : Ideal S` lying over `p : Ideal R` is the degree of the
extension `(S / P) : (R / p)`.

We do not assume `P` lies over `p` in the definition; we return `0` instead.

See `inertiaDeg_algebraMap` for the common case where `f = algebraMap R S`
and there is an algebra structure `R / p → S / P`.

Ideal.FinrankQuotientMap.linearIndepende.code:
Ideal.FinrankQuotientMap.linearIndependent_of_nontrivial.{u, v, u_1, u_3, u_4, u_5, u_6} {R : Type u} [CommRing R]
  {S : Type v} [CommRing S] [Algebra R S] (K : Type u_1) [Field K] [Algebra R K] [hRK : IsFractionRing R K]
  {V : Type u_3} {V' : Type u_4} {V'' : Type u_5} [AddCommGroup V] [Module R V] [Module K V] [IsScalarTower R K V]
  [AddCommGroup V'] [Module R V'] [Module S V'] [IsScalarTower R S V'] [AddCommGroup V''] [Module R V'']
  [IsDedekindDomain R] (hRS : RingHom.ker (algebraMap R S) ≠ ⊤) (f : V'' →ₗ[R] V) (hf : Function.Injective ⇑f)
  (f' : V'' →ₗ[R] V') {ι : Type u_6} {b : ι → V''} (hb' : LinearIndependent S (⇑f' ∘ b)) : LinearIndependent K (⇑f ∘ b)
Ideal.FinrankQuotientMap.linearIndepende.comment:
Let `V` be a vector space over `K = Frac(R)`, `S / R` a ring extension
and `V'` a module over `S`. If `b`, in the intersection `V''` of `V` and `V'`,
is linear independent over `S` in `V'`, then it is linear independent over `R` in `V`.

The statement we prove is actually slightly more general:
 * it suffices that the inclusion `algebraMap R S : R → S` is nontrivial
 * the function `f' : V'' → V'` doesn't need to be injective

explanatories.LinearIndependent: This definition characterizes a family of vectors as linearly independent over a specified ring if no vector in the family can be expressed as a linear combination of the others.

Ideal.FinrankQuotientMap.linearIndepende.description: This theorem states that if a set of vectors is linearly independent over a ring extension and the map to another vector space is injective, then the same set of vectors remains linearly independent over the original ring.

Ideal.FinrankQuotientMap.span_eq_top.code:
Ideal.FinrankQuotientMap.span_eq_top.{u, v, u_1, u_2} {R : Type u} [CommRing R] {S : Type v} [CommRing S] (p : Ideal R)
  [Algebra R S] {K : Type u_1} [Field K] [Algebra R K] {L : Type u_2} [Field L] [Algebra S L] [IsFractionRing S L]
  [IsDomain R] [IsDomain S] [Algebra K L] [IsNoetherian R S] [Algebra R L] [IsScalarTower R S L] [IsScalarTower R K L]
  [IsIntegralClosure S R L] [NoZeroSMulDivisors R K] (hp : p ≠ ⊤) (b : Set S)
  (hb' : Submodule.span R b ⊔ Submodule.restrictScalars R (map (algebraMap R S) p) = ⊤) :
  Submodule.span K (⇑(algebraMap S L) '' b) = ⊤
Ideal.FinrankQuotientMap.span_eq_top.comment:
If `b` mod `p` spans `S/p` as `R/p`-space, then `b` itself spans `Frac(S)` as `K`-space.

Here,
* `p` is an ideal of `R` such that `R / p` is nontrivial
* `K` is a field that has an embedding of `R` (in particular we can take `K = Frac(R)`)
* `L` is a field extension of `K`
* `S` is the integral closure of `R` in `L`

More precisely, we avoid quotients in this statement and instead require that `b ∪ pS` spans `S`.

Ideal.finrank_quotient_map.{u, v, u_1, u_2} {R : Type u} [CommRing R] {S : Type v} [CommRing S] (p : Ideal R)
  [Algebra R S] (K : Type u_1) [Field K] [Algebra R K] [hRK : IsFractionRing R K] (L : Type u_2) [Field L] [Algebra S L]
  [IsFractionRing S L] [IsDomain S] [IsDedekindDomain R] [Algebra K L] [Algebra R L] [IsScalarTower R K L]
  [IsScalarTower R S L] [IsIntegralClosure S R L] [hp : p.IsMaximal] [IsNoetherian R S] :
  finrank (R ⧸ p) (S ⧸ map (algebraMap R S) p) = finrank K L
Ideal.finrank_quotient_map.comment:
If `p` is a maximal ideal of `R`, and `S` is the integral closure of `R` in `L`,
then the dimension `[S/pS : R/p]` is equal to `[Frac(S) : Frac(R)]`.

of `P` over `p`.

explanatories.Ideal.le_pow_ramificationIdx: This theorem states that the image of an ideal under a ring homomorphism is contained in the ideal raised to the power of its ramification index.

explanatories.Ideal.Quotient.algebraQuotientOfLEComap: If a certain ideal in one ring is contained within the preimage of another ideal under a ring homomorphism, then there exists a natural algebra structure connecting the quotients of these two ideals.

Ideal.rank_pow_quot_aux.{u, v} {R : Type u} [CommRing R] {S : Type v} [CommRing S] (f : R →+* S) (p : Ideal R)
  (P : Ideal S) [hfp : NeZero e] [IsDedekindDomain S] [p.IsMaximal] [P.IsPrime] (hP0 : P ≠ ⊥) {i : ℕ} (hi : i < e) :
  Module.rank (R ⧸ p) ↥(map (Quotient.mk (P ^ e)) (P ^ i)) =
    Module.rank (R ⧸ p) (S ⧸ P) + Module.rank (R ⧸ p) ↥(map (Quotient.mk (P ^ e)) (P ^ (i + 1)))
Ideal.rank_pow_quot_aux.comment:
Since the inclusion `(P^(i + 1) / P^e) ⊂ (P^i / P^e)` has a kernel isomorphic to `P / S`,
`[P^i / P^e : R / p] = [P^(i+1) / P^e : R / p] + [P / S : R / p]`

**Chinese remainder theorem** for a ring of integers: if the prime ideal `p : Ideal R`
factors in `S` as `∏ i, P i ^ e i`, then `S ⧸ I` factors as `Π i, R ⧸ (P i ^ e i)`.

Ideal.sum_ramification_inertia.{u, v, u_1, u_2} {R : Type u} [CommRing R] {S : Type v} [CommRing S] (p : Ideal R)
  [IsDedekindDomain S] [Algebra R S] (K : Type u_1) (L : Type u_2) [Field K] [Field L] [IsDedekindDomain R]
  [Algebra R K] [IsFractionRing R K] [Algebra S L] [IsFractionRing S L] [Algebra K L] [Algebra R L]
  [IsScalarTower R S L] [IsScalarTower R K L] [IsNoetherian R S] [IsIntegralClosure S R L] [p.IsMaximal] (hp0 : p ≠ ⊥) :
  ∑ P ∈ (factors (map (algebraMap R S) p)).toFinset,
      ramificationIdx (algebraMap R S) p P * inertiaDeg (algebraMap R S) p P =
    finrank K L
Ideal.sum_ramification_inertia.comment:
The **fundamental identity** of ramification index `e` and inertia degree `f`:
for `P` ranging over the primes lying over `p`, `∑ P, e P * f P = [Frac(S) : Frac(R)]`;
here `S` is a finite `R`-module (and thus `Frac(S) : Frac(R)` is a finite extension) and `p`
is maximal.

explanatories.Multiset.toFinset: This definition describes a function that transforms a multiset into a finite set by eliminating any duplicate elements.

ideal.sum_ramification_inertia.description: This theorem establishes a fundamental relationship between the ramification indices and inertia degrees of prime ideals over a maximal ideal, asserting that the weighted sum of these values equals the finite degree of the extensions of the fraction fields.

Rat.MulRingNorm.eq_on_nat_iff_eq_on_Int.code: Rat.MulRingNorm.eq_on_nat_iff_eq_on_Int {f g : MulRingNorm ℚ} : (∀ (n : ℕ), f ↑n = g ↑n) ↔ ∀ (n : ℤ), f ↑n = g ↑n
Rat.MulRingNorm.eq_on_nat_iff_eq_on_Int.comment:
Values of a multiplicative norm of the rationals coincide on ℕ if and only if they coincide
on `ℤ`.
Rat.MulRingNorm.eq_on_nat_iff_eq_on_Int.description: The values of a multiplicative norm for rational numbers are equal on natural numbers if and only if they are equal on integers.

Rat.MulRingNorm.mulRingNorm_padic.comment: The mulRingNorm corresponding to the p-adic norm on `ℚ`.

explanatories.Nat.Prime: This definition specifies the criterion for a natural number to be classified as prime, requiring it to be at least two and have only one and itself as divisors.
explanatories.padicNorm.zero: This theorem states that the p-adic norm of zero is equal to zero.
explanatories.Rat.cast_zero: The theorem establishes that the cast of zero into a division ring is equal to zero.
explanatories.padicNorm.triangle_ineq: This theorem states that the p-adic norm satisfies the triangle inequality, indicating that the norm of the sum of two rational numbers is less than or equal to the sum of their individual norms.
explanatories.forall_const: For any nonempty type, a constant function to a proposition is equivalent to that proposition itself.
explanatories.padicNorm.neg: This theorem asserts that the p-adic norm is symmetric, meaning the p-adic norm of a rational number and its negative are equal.
explanatories.ne_eq: The theorem demonstrates that the inequality of two elements is equivalent to the negation of their equality.
explanatories.one_ne_zero: This theorem demonstrates that one is not equal to zero in any type that supports both one and zero.
explanatories.not_false_eq_true: The theorem states that the negation of a false proposition is equivalent to a true proposition.
explanatories.padicNorm.eq_zpow_of_nonzero: This theorem shows that for a non-zero rational number, the p-adic norm can be expressed as a power of p determined by the p-adic valuation of the number.
explanatories.padicValRat.one: The theorem asserts that the p-adic valuation of one is zero for any prime in the context of rational numbers.
explanatories.neg_zero: This theorem states that in a type with a negation operation and zero element, the negation of zero is equal to zero.
explanatories.zpow_zero: This theorem establishes that raising any element of a division inverse monoid to the power of zero yields the identity element of the monoid.
explanatories.Rat.cast_one: The theorem establishes that the cast of one into a division ring is equal to one.
explanatories.padicNorm.mul: This theorem states that the p-adic norm is multiplicative, meaning the norm of the product of two rational numbers equals the product of their norms.
explanatories.Rat.cast_mul: The theorem states that the image of the product of two rational numbers in a division ring with characteristic zero is equal to the product of their respective images.
explanatories.Rat.cast_eq_zero: The theorem asserts that a rational number is equal to zero if and only if its image in a division ring with characteristic zero is also zero.
explanatories.padicNorm.zero_of_padicNorm_eq_zero: This theorem establishes that if the p-adic norm of a rational number is zero, then the rational number itself must also be zero.
explanatories.Nat.cast_zero: The theorem states that the natural number zero is equal to the additive identity in any type that possesses an additive monoid structure with a multiplicative identity.
explanatories.Nat.cast_eq_zero: This theorem demonstrates that in a type with characteristic zero and an additive monoid with a unity element, the equality of the image of a natural number under the canonical map to zero is equivalent to the natural number itself being zero.
explanatories.Nat.cast_one: The theorem asserts that the natural number one, when cast into an additive monoid with a unity element, is equal to the identity element of that monoid.
explanatories.Nat.cast_mul: This theorem states that the natural number multiplication operation is compatible with the operation of multiplication in a non-associative semiring when interpreted in that structure.

Rat.MulRingNorm.mulRingNorm_padic.fullDefinition: def mulRingNorm_padic (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] : MulRingNorm ℚ := { toFun     := fun x : ℚ ↦ (padicNorm p x : ℝ),   map_zero' := by simp only [padicNorm.zero, Rat.cast_zero]   add_le'   := by simp only; norm_cast; exact fun r s ↦ padicNorm.triangle_ineq r s   neg'      := by simp only [forall_const, padicNorm.neg]   eq_zero_of_map_eq_zero' := by     simp only [Rat.cast_eq_zero]     apply padicNorm.zero_of_padicNorm_eq_zero   map_one' := by simp only [ne_eq, one_ne_zero, not_false_eq_true, padicNorm.eq_zpow_of_nonzero,     padicValRat.one, neg_zero, zpow_zero, Rat.cast_one]   map_mul' := by simp only [padicNorm.mul, Rat.cast_mul, forall_const] }
Rat.MulRingNorm.mulRingNorm_padic.description: The multiplicative norm associated with the p-adic norm for rational numbers is defined.

Rat.MulRingNorm.eq_on_nat_iff_eq.code: Rat.MulRingNorm.eq_on_nat_iff_eq {f g : MulRingNorm ℚ} : (∀ (n : ℕ), f ↑n = g ↑n) ↔ f = g

Rat.MulRingNorm.eq_on_nat_iff_eq.description: The equality of two multiplicative norms for rational numbers is fully determined by their values on natural numbers.

Nat.Prime.sq_add_sq.comment:

of two squares. Also known as **Fermat's Christmas theorem**.
Nat.Prime.sq_add_sq.description: The theorem establishes that any prime number not congruent to three modulo four can be expressed as the sum of two square numbers.

nat.eq_sq_add_sq_iff_eq_sq_mul.code: Nat.eq_sq_add_sq_iff_eq_sq_mul {n : ℕ} : (∃ x y, n = x ^ 2 + y ^ 2) ↔ ∃ a b, n = a ^ 2 * b ∧ IsSquare (-1)
nat.eq_sq_add_sq_iff_eq_sq_mul.comment:
A natural number `n` is a sum of two squares if and only if `n = a^2 * b` with natural
numbers `a` and `b` such that `-1` is a square modulo `b`.

explanatories.IsSquare: An element of a multiplicative type is considered a perfect square if it can be expressed as the product of some element with itself.

nat.eq_sq_add_sq_iff_eq_sq_mul.description: The theorem asserts that a natural number can be expressed as the sum of two squares if and only if it can be represented as the product of a square and another natural number, with the condition that negative one is a perfect square in the modular context of that other number.

Nat.eq_sq_add_sq_iff.code: Nat.eq_sq_add_sq_iff {n : ℕ} : (∃ x y, n = x ^ 2 + y ^ 2) ↔ ∀ {q : ℕ}, Nat.Prime q → q % 4 = 3 → Even (padicValNat q n)
Nat.eq_sq_add_sq_iff.comment:
A (positive) natural number `n` is a sum of two squares if and only if the exponent of
every prime `q` such that `q % 4 = 3` in the prime factorization of `n` is even.
(The assumption `0 < n` is not present, since for `n = 0`, both sides are satisfied;
the right hand side holds, since `padicValNat q 0 = 0` by definition.)

explanatories.Even: An element of an additive type is classified as even if it can be represented as the sum of some element with itself.

Nat.eq_sq_add_sq_iff.description: A positive natural number can be expressed as the sum of two squares if and only if all primes congruent to three modulo four in its prime factorization have even exponents.

conductor.code: conductor.{u_1, u_2} (R : Type u_1) {S : Type u_2} [CommRing R] [CommRing S] [Algebra R S] (x : S) : Ideal S
conductor.comment:
Let `S / R` be a ring extension and `x : S`, then the conductor of `R<x>` is the
biggest ideal of `S` contained in `R<x>`.

explanatories.Ideal: An ideal in a semiring is an additive submonoid that is closed under multiplication by elements from the semiring.
explanatories.add_mul: This theorem defines the right distributive property of multiplication over addition in a specific algebraic structure.
explanatories.Subalgebra.add_mem: The sum of two elements in a subalgebra is also an element of that subalgebra.
explanatories.MulZeroClass.zero_mul: This theorem establishes that multiplying any element by zero results in zero, demonstrating that zero acts as a left absorbing element in multiplication.
explanatories.Subalgebra.zero_mem: The zero element is included in every subalgebra.
explanatories.smul_eq_mul: This theorem establishes that the scalar multiplication of two elements is equivalent to their multiplication in a type that has a multiplication operation.
explanatories.mul_left_comm: The theorem establishes that in a commutative semigroup, the multiplication operation can be rearranged among three elements without changing the result.
explanatories.mul_assoc: This theorem asserts that multiplication in a semigroup is associative, meaning the product of three elements is the same regardless of how they are grouped.
explanatories.Algebra.id.smul_eq_mul: This theorem establishes that scalar multiplication by an element in a commutative semiring is equivalent to the usual multiplication of that element with another element from the same semiring.
explanatories.Ideal.add_mem: The sum of any two elements in an ideal of a semiring is also contained within that ideal.
explanatories.Ideal.zero_mem: The zero element belongs to any ideal in a semiring.

conductor.fullDefinition: def conductor (x : S) : Ideal S where   carrier := {a | ∀ b : S, a * b ∈ R<x>}   zero_mem' b := by simpa only [zero_mul] using Subalgebra.zero_mem _   add_mem' ha hb c := by simpa only [add_mul] using Subalgebra.add_mem _ (ha c) (hb c)   smul_mem' c a ha b := by simpa only [smul_eq_mul, mul_left_comm, mul_assoc] using ha (c * b)
conductor.description: This defines the conductor of a ring extension as the largest ideal of the extension ring that is contained within the corresponding subring generated by the base ring and an element from the extension.

conductor_eq_of_eq.code:
conductor_eq_of_eq.{u_1, u_2} {R : Type u_1} {S : Type u_2} [CommRing R] [CommRing S] [Algebra R S] {x y : S}
  (h : ↑(adjoin R {x}) = ↑(adjoin R {y})) : conductor R x = conductor R y
conductor_eq_of_eq.description: If two elements both generate the same subring extension, then their corresponding conductors are equal.

conductor_subset_adjoin.code:
conductor_subset_adjoin.{u_1, u_2} {R : Type u_1} {S : Type u_2} [CommRing R] [CommRing S] [Algebra R S] {x : S} :
  ↑(conductor R x) ⊆ ↑(adjoin R {x})
conductor_subset_adjoin.description: The conductor of an element in a ring extension is contained within the subring generated by that element.

mem_conductor_iff.code:
mem_conductor_iff.{u_1, u_2} {R : Type u_1} {S : Type u_2} [CommRing R] [CommRing S] [Algebra R S] {x y : S} :
  y ∈ conductor R x ↔ ∀ (b : S), y * b ∈ adjoin R {x}

explanatories.Algebra.adjoin: The adjoin operation defines the smallest subalgebra containing a given set of elements from an algebra over a commutative semiring.

mem_conductor_iff.description: An element belongs to the conductor of an element in a ring extension if and only if it multiplies with any element from the extension to produce another element in the subring generated by that initial element.

  {x : S} (h : adjoin R {x} = ⊤) : conductor R x = ⊤

explanatories.Algebra.adjoin: The adjoin operation defines the smallest subalgebra containing a given set of elements from an algebra over a commutative semiring.

conductor_eq_top_of_adjoin_eq_top.description: If the subalgebra generated by an element in a ring extension is the entire ring, then the conductor of that element is also the entire ring.

prod_mem_ideal_map_of_mem_conductor.code:
prod_mem_ideal_map_of_mem_conductor.{u_1, u_2} {R : Type u_1} {S : Type u_2} [CommRing R] [CommRing S] [Algebra R S]
  {x : S} {I : Ideal R} {p : R} {z : S} (hp : p ∈ comap (algebraMap R S) (conductor R x))
  (hz' : z ∈ Ideal.map (algebraMap R S) I) :

This technical lemma tell us that if `C` is the conductor of `R<x>` and `I` is an ideal of `R`
then `p * (I * S) ⊆ I * R<x>` for any `p` in `C ∩ R`

quotAdjoinEquivQuotMap.code:
quotAdjoinEquivQuotMap.{u_1, u_2} {R : Type u_1} {S : Type u_2} [CommRing R] [CommRing S] [Algebra R S] {x : S}
  {I : Ideal R} (hx : comap (algebraMap R S) (conductor R x) ⊔ I = ⊤)
  (h_alg : Function.Injective ⇑(algebraMap (↥(adjoin R {x})) S)) :

quotAdjoinEquivQuotMap.comment:
The canonical morphism of rings from `R<x> ⧸ (I*R<x>)` to `S ⧸ (I*S)` is an isomorphism
when `I` and `(conductor R x) ∩ R` are coprime.

explanatories.Ideal.Quotient.lift: A ring homomorphism that maps all elements of an ideal to zero can be extended to a homomorphism from the quotient of the ring by that ideal.
explanatories.Ideal.Quotient.mk: A ring homomorphism from a commutative ring to its quotient by an ideal maps elements of the original ring to their respective equivalence classes in the quotient ring.
explanatories.RingHom.comp_apply: This theorem asserts that the composition of two ring homomorphisms applied to an element is equal to the application of the second homomorphism followed by the application of the first homomorphism.
explanatories.Ideal.Quotient.eq_zero_iff_mem: An element from a ring maps to zero in the quotient by an ideal if and only if it belongs to that ideal.
explanatories.RingEquiv.ofBijective: This constructs a ring isomorphism between two non-unital non-associative semirings from a bijective ring homomorphism between them.
explanatories.RingHom.lift_injective_of_ker_le_ideal: The induced map from the quotient of a ring by a specified ideal is injective if the kernel of the ring homomorphism is contained within that ideal and the homomorphism sends the ideal's elements to zero.
explanatories.RingHom.mem_ker: An element belongs to the kernel of a ring homomorphism if and only if it maps to zero under that homomorphism.
explanatories.Ideal.Quotient.lift_surjective_of_surjec: If a ring homomorphism from a commutative ring to a semiring is surjective and maps elements of the ideal to zero, then the induced homomorphism from the quotient ring is also surjective.
explanatories.Ideal.Quotient.mk_surjective: The canonical mapping from a commutative ring to its quotient by an ideal is surjective, meaning every element in the quotient has a preimage in the original ring.
explanatories.Submodule.mem_top: This theorem states that every element of a module is a member of the entire module itself.
explanatories.Ideal.map_sup: The image of the sup of two ideals under a ring homomorphism is equal to the sup of the images of each ideal under the same homomorphism.
explanatories.RingHom.map_one: This theorem states that a ring homomorphism must map the multiplicative identity element of its domain to the multiplicative identity element of its codomain.
explanatories.sup_le_sup: The supremum of two elements is less than or equal to the supremum of their respective upper bounds.
explanatories.Ideal.map_comap_le: The image of the preimage of an ideal under a ring homomorphism is contained in the original ideal.
explanatories.le_refl: This theorem confirms that in a preorder, any element is related to itself under the less than or equal relation.
explanatories.Ideal.mem_quotient_iff_mem_sup: An element in the quotient of a ring by an ideal belongs to the image of the map to another ideal if and only if it is contained in the join of that ideal and the original ideal.
explanatories.Ideal.mem_map_iff_of_surjective: An element is in the image of an ideal under a surjective function if and only if there exists an element in the ideal such that applying the function to it yields the element in question.

explanatories.Function.comp_apply: The composition of two functions applied to an argument is equal to applying the first function to the result of applying the second function to that argument.

quotAdjoinEquivQuotMap.fullDefinition: noncomputable def quotAdjoinEquivQuotMap (hx : (conductor R x).comap (algebraMap R S) ⊔ I = ⊤)     (h_alg : Function.Injective (algebraMap R<x> S)) :     R<x> ⧸ I.map (algebraMap R R<x>) ≃+* S ⧸ I.map (algebraMap R S) := by   let f : R<x> ⧸ I.map (algebraMap R R<x>) →+* S ⧸ I.map (algebraMap R S) :=     (Ideal.Quotient.lift (I.map (algebraMap R R<x>))       ((Ideal.Quotient.mk (I.map (algebraMap R S))).comp (algebraMap R<x> S)) (fun r hr => by       have : algebraMap R S = (algebraMap R<x> S).comp (algebraMap R R<x>) := by ext; rfl       rw [RingHom.comp_apply, Ideal.Quotient.eq_zero_iff_mem, this, ← Ideal.map_map]       exact Ideal.mem_map_of_mem _ hr))   refine RingEquiv.ofBijective f ⟨?_, ?_⟩   · --the kernel of the map is clearly `(I * S) ∩ R<x>`. To get injectivity, we need to show that     --this is contained in `I * R<x>`, which is the content of the previous lemma.     refine RingHom.lift_injective_of_ker_le_ideal _ _ fun u hu => ?_     rwa [RingHom.mem_ker, RingHom.comp_apply, Ideal.Quotient.eq_zero_iff_mem, ← Ideal.mem_comap,       comap_map_eq_map_adjoin_of_coprime_conductor hx h_alg] at hu   · -- Surjectivity follows from the surjectivity of the canonical map `R<x> → S ⧸ (I * S)`,     -- which in turn follows from the fact that `I * S + (conductor R x) = S`.     refine Ideal.Quotient.lift_surjective_of_surjective _ _ fun y => ?_     obtain ⟨z, hz⟩ := Ideal.Quotient.mk_surjective y     have : z ∈ conductor R x ⊔ I.map (algebraMap R S) := by       suffices conductor R x ⊔ I.map (algebraMap R S) = ⊤ by simp only [this, Submodule.mem_top]       rw [Ideal.eq_top_iff_one] at hx ⊢       replace hx := Ideal.mem_map_of_mem (algebraMap R S) hx       rw [Ideal.map_sup, RingHom.map_one] at hx       exact (sup_le_sup         (show ((conductor R x).comap (algebraMap R S)).map (algebraMap R S) ≤ conductor R x           from Ideal.map_comap_le)           (le_refl (I.map (algebraMap R S)))) hx     rw [← Ideal.mem_quotient_iff_mem_sup, hz, Ideal.mem_map_iff_of_surjective] at this     · obtain ⟨u, hu, hu'⟩ := this       use ⟨u, conductor_subset_adjoin hu⟩       simp only [← hu']       rfl     · exact Ideal.Quotient.mk_surjective
quotAdjoinEquivQuotMap.description: The quotient of the subring generated by an element and an ideal in a ring extension is isomorphic to the quotient of the target ring and a corresponding ideal under certain conditions related to injectivity and coprimality of ideals.

explanatories.Ideal.Quotient.mk: A ring homomorphism from a commutative ring to its quotient by an ideal maps elements of the original ring to their respective equivalence classes in the quotient ring.
explanatories.RingHom.comp_apply: This theorem asserts that the composition of two ring homomorphisms applied to an element is equal to the application of the second homomorphism followed by the application of the first homomorphism.
explanatories.Ideal.Quotient.eq_zero_iff_mem: An element from a ring maps to zero in the quotient by an ideal if and only if it belongs to that ideal.
explanatories.RingEquiv.ofBijective: This constructs a ring isomorphism between two non-unital non-associative semirings from a bijective ring homomorphism between them.
explanatories.RingHom.lift_injective_of_ker_le_ideal: The induced map from the quotient of a ring by a specified ideal is injective if the kernel of the ring homomorphism is contained within that ideal and the homomorphism sends the ideal's elements to zero.
explanatories.RingHom.mem_ker: An element belongs to the kernel of a ring homomorphism if and only if it maps to zero under that homomorphism.
explanatories.Ideal.Quotient.lift_surjective_of_surjec: If a ring homomorphism from a commutative ring to a semiring is surjective and maps elements of the ideal to zero, then the induced homomorphism from the quotient ring is also surjective.
explanatories.Ideal.Quotient.mk_surjective: The canonical mapping from a commutative ring to its quotient by an ideal is surjective, meaning every element in the quotient has a preimage in the original ring.
explanatories.Submodule.mem_top: This theorem states that every element of a module is a member of the entire module itself.
explanatories.Ideal.map_sup: The image of the sup of two ideals under a ring homomorphism is equal to the sup of the images of each ideal under the same homomorphism.
explanatories.RingHom.map_one: This theorem states that a ring homomorphism must map the multiplicative identity element of its domain to the multiplicative identity element of its codomain.
explanatories.sup_le_sup: The supremum of two elements is less than or equal to the supremum of their respective upper bounds.
explanatories.Ideal.map_comap_le: The image of the preimage of an ideal under a ring homomorphism is contained in the original ideal.
explanatories.le_refl: This theorem confirms that in a preorder, any element is related to itself under the less than or equal relation.

quot_adjoin_equiv_quot_map.fullDefinition: noncomputable def quotAdjoinEquivQuotMap (hx : (conductor R x).comap (algebraMap R S) ⊔ I = ⊤)     (h_alg : Function.Injective (algebraMap R<x> S)) :     R<x> ⧸ I.map (algebraMap R R<x>) ≃+* S ⧸ I.map (algebraMap R S) := by   let f : R<x> ⧸ I.map (algebraMap R R<x>) →+* S ⧸ I.map (algebraMap R S) :=     (Ideal.Quotient.lift (I.map (algebraMap R R<x>))       ((Ideal.Quotient.mk (I.map (algebraMap R S))).comp (algebraMap R<x> S)) (fun r hr => by       have : algebraMap R S = (algebraMap R<x> S).comp (algebraMap R R<x>) := by ext; rfl       rw [RingHom.comp_apply, Ideal.Quotient.eq_zero_iff_mem, this, ← Ideal.map_map]       exact Ideal.mem_map_of_mem _ hr))   refine RingEquiv.ofBijective f ⟨?_, ?_⟩   · --the kernel of the map is clearly `(I * S) ∩ R<x>`. To get injectivity, we need to show that     --this is contained in `I * R<x>`, which is the content of the previous lemma.     refine RingHom.lift_injective_of_ker_le_ideal _ _ fun u hu => ?_     rwa [RingHom.mem_ker, RingHom.comp_apply, Ideal.Quotient.eq_zero_iff_mem, ← Ideal.mem_comap,       comap_map_eq_map_adjoin_of_coprime_conductor hx h_alg] at hu   · -- Surjectivity follows from the surjectivity of the canonical map `R<x> → S ⧸ (I * S)`,     -- which in turn follows from the fact that `I * S + (conductor R x) = S`.     refine Ideal.Quotient.lift_surjective_of_surjective _ _ fun y => ?_     obtain ⟨z, hz⟩ := Ideal.Quotient.mk_surjective y     have : z ∈ conductor R x ⊔ I.map (algebraMap R S) := by       suffices conductor R x ⊔ I.map (algebraMap R S) = ⊤ by simp only [this, Submodule.mem_top]       rw [Ideal.eq_top_iff_one] at hx ⊢       replace hx := Ideal.mem_map_of_mem (algebraMap R S) hx       rw [Ideal.map_sup, RingHom.map_one] at hx       exact (sup_le_sup         (show ((conductor R x).comap (algebraMap R S)).map (algebraMap R S) ≤ conductor R x           from Ideal.map_comap_le)           (le_refl (I.map (algebraMap R S)))) hx     rw [← Ideal.mem_quotient_iff_mem_sup, hz, Ideal.mem_map_iff_of_surjective] at this     · obtain ⟨u, hu, hu'⟩ := this       use ⟨u, conductor_subset_adjoin hu⟩       simp only [← hu']       rfl     · exact Ideal.Quotient.mk_surjective

KummerDedekind.normalizedFactorsMapEquivNormalizedFactorsMinPolyMk.{u_1, u_2} {R : Type u_1} {S : Type u_2} [CommRing R]
  [CommRing S] [Algebra R S] {x : S} {I : Ideal R} [IsDomain R] [IsIntegrallyClosed R] [IsDedekindDomain S]
  [NoZeroSMulDivisors R S] (hI : I.IsMaximal) (hI' : I ≠ ⊥) (hx : comap (algebraMap R S) (conductor R x) ⊔ I = ⊤)

KummerDedekind.normalizedFactorsMapEquiv.comment:
The first half of the **Kummer-Dedekind Theorem** in the monogenic case, stating that the prime
factors of `I*S` are in bijection with those of the minimal polynomial of the generator of `S`
over `R`, taken `mod I`.

explanatories.LSeriesSummable.LSeriesHasSum: This theorem states that if a sequence is L-series summable at a complex point, then it has a specific L-series sum represented by the evaluation of the series at that point.

LSeriesHasSum_iff.description: This theorem states that a function has an L-series that converges to a specific complex value if and only if it is summable at that point and the value of the L-series at that point equals the specified complex value.

LSeriesSummable_congr.code:
LSeriesSummable_congr {f g : ℕ → ℂ} (s : ℂ) (h : ∀ {n : ℕ}, n ≠ 0 → f n = g n) :

LSeriesSummable_congr.description: This theorem asserts that if two sequences are equal at all non-zero indices, then their corresponding L-series sums are either both convergent or both divergent at a given complex number.

LSeries_congr.code: LSeries_congr {f g : ℕ → ℂ} (s : ℂ) (h : ∀ {n : ℕ}, n ≠ 0 → f n = g n) : LSeries f s = LSeries g s
LSeries_congr.description: This theorem states that if two sequences are equal at all positive indices, then their L-series are also equal when evaluated at the same complex point.

LSeries.notation.«term↗_».comment:
We introduce notation `↗f` for `f` interpreted as a function `ℕ → ℂ`.

Let `R` be a ring with a coercion to `ℂ`. Then we can write `↗χ` when `χ : DirichletCharacter R`
or `↗f` when `f : ArithmeticFunction R` or simply `f : N → R` with a coercion from `ℕ` to `N`
as an argument to `LSeries`, `LSeriesHasSum`, `LSeriesSummable` etc.

LSeries.delta.comment: The indicator function of `{1} ⊆ ℕ` with values in `ℂ`.
LSeries.delta.fullDefinition: def LSeries.delta (n : ℕ) : ℂ :=   if n = 1 then 1 else 0
LSeries.delta.description: This definition describes a function that takes a natural number and returns a complex value, specifically indicating whether that number is in the set containing only the number one.

LSeries.mul_delta_eq_smul_delta.code: LSeries.mul_delta_eq_smul_delta {f : ℕ → ℂ} : f * δ = f 1 • δ
LSeries.mul_delta_eq_smul_delta.description: This theorem states that multiplying a sequence by a delta function is equivalent to scaling the delta function by the value of the sequence at index one.

LSeries.mul_delta.code: LSeries.mul_delta {f : ℕ → ℂ} (h : f 1 = 1) : f * δ = δ
LSeries.mul_delta.description: This theorem shows that if a function evaluates to one at a specific point, then the product of the function and a delta function equals the delta function.

LSeries.term_delta.code: LSeries.term_delta (s : ℂ) (n : ℕ) : term δ s n = if n = 1 then 1 else 0

explanatories.Lean.Parser.Category.term: The term category in Lean represents the syntax for expressions in type theory, distinguishing between raw term syntax and their elaborated expression forms.

LSeries.term_delta.description: This theorem defines the term of a delta function in an L-series, stating that it equals one when evaluated at one and is zero otherwise.

LSeriesSummable.le_const_mul_rpow.code:
LSeriesSummable.le_const_mul_rpow {f : ℕ → ℂ} {s : ℂ} (h : LSeriesSummable f s) :
  ∃ C, ∀ (n : ℕ), n ≠ 0 → ‖f n‖ ≤ C * ↑n ^ s.re
LSeriesSummable.le_const_mul_rpow.comment:
If the `LSeries` of `f` is summable at `s`, then `f n` is bounded in absolute value
by a constant times `n^(re s)`.

explanatories.Complex.re: This defines a function that extracts the real component from a complex number.
explanatories.LSeriesHasSum.LSeriesSummable: This theorem asserts that if a sequence has a specific L-series sum at a complex point, then the sequence is L-series summable at that point.

LSeriesSummable.le_const_mul_rpow.description: This theorem states that if the L-series of a sequence is summable at a certain complex point, then the absolute value of the terms in the sequence is bounded by a constant multiplied by the real part of that point raised to the power of the index.

LSeriesSummable_of_le_const_mul_rpow.code:
LSeriesSummable_of_le_const_mul_rpow {f : ℕ → ℂ} {x : ℝ} {s : ℂ} (hs : x < s.re)
  (h : ∃ C, ∀ (n : ℕ), n ≠ 0 → ‖f n‖ ≤ C * ↑n ^ (x - 1)) : LSeriesSummable f s
LSeriesSummable_of_le_const_mul_rpow.comment:
If `f n` is bounded in absolute value by a constant times `n^(x-1)` and `re s > x`,
then the `LSeries` of `f` is summable at `s`.

explanatories.LSeriesHasSum.LSeriesSummable: This theorem asserts that if a sequence has a specific L-series sum at a complex point, then the sequence is L-series summable at that point.

LSeriesSummable_of_le_const_mul_rpow.description: If a sequence is bounded by a constant multiplied by a polynomial term and evaluated at a complex point where the real part exceeds a certain threshold, then its L-series converges absolutely at that point.

LSeriesSummable_of_bounded_of_one_lt_re {f : ℕ → ℂ} {m : ℝ} (h : ∀ (n : ℕ), n ≠ 0 → Complex.abs (f n) ≤ m) {s : ℂ}

LSeriesSummable_of_bounded_of_one_lt_re.description: This theorem establishes that if a sequence is bounded and the real part of a complex point is greater than one, then its L-series converges absolutely at that point.

nat.arithmetic_function.l_series_summabl.description: This theorem establishes that if a sequence is bounded and the real part of a complex point is greater than one, then its L-series converges absolutely at that point.

LSeries.term_add.code: LSeries.term_add (f g : ℕ → ℂ) (s : ℂ) : term (f + g) s = term f s + term g s
LSeries.term_add.description: This theorem demonstrates that the term associated with the sum of two sequences at a complex point equals the sum of the terms of each sequence at that point.

LSeries.term_add_apply.code: LSeries.term_add_apply (f g : ℕ → ℂ) (s : ℂ) (n : ℕ) : term (f + g) s n = term f s n + term g s n
LSeries.term_add_apply.description: This theorem states that the nth term of the sum of two sequences at a complex point is equal to the sum of the nth terms of each sequence at that point.

LSeries_add.code:
LSeries_add {f g : ℕ → ℂ} {s : ℂ} (hf : LSeriesSummable f s) (hg : LSeriesSummable g s) :
  LSeries (f + g) s = LSeries f s + LSeries g s

explanatories.LSeriesSummable: This definition indicates that a sequence is considered L-series summable at a complex point if its L-series converges absolutely at that point.

LSeries_add.description: This theorem establishes that the series obtained from the sum of two summable sequences at a complex point is equal to the sum of the series derived from each sequence at that point.

nat.arithmetic_function.l_series_add.code:
LSeries_add {f g : ℕ → ℂ} {s : ℂ} (hf : LSeriesSummable f s) (hg : LSeriesSummable g s) :
  LSeries (f + g) s = LSeries f s + LSeries g s

explanatories.LSeriesSummable: This definition indicates that a sequence is considered L-series summable at a complex point if its L-series converges absolutely at that point.

nat.arithmetic_function.l_series_add.description: This theorem establishes that the series obtained from the sum of two summable sequences at a complex point is equal to the sum of the series derived from each sequence at that point.

LSeries.term_neg.code: LSeries.term_neg (f : ℕ → ℂ) (s : ℂ) : term (-f) s = -term f s
LSeries.term_neg.description: This theorem asserts that the term associated with the negation of a sequence at a complex point is equal to the negation of the term of the original sequence at that point.

LSeriesSummable.neg.code: LSeriesSummable.neg {f : ℕ → ℂ} {s : ℂ} (hf : LSeriesSummable f s) : LSeriesSummable (-f) s

explanatories.HasSum.neg: If a function has a particular infinite sum, then the function whose values are the negation of those values has an infinite sum equal to the negation of the original sum.

LSeriesSummable.neg.description: This theorem states that if a sequence is L-series summable at a complex point, then the negation of that sequence is also L-series summable at the same point.

LSeries.term_neg_apply.code: LSeries.term_neg_apply (f : ℕ → ℂ) (s : ℂ) (n : ℕ) : term (-f) s n = -term f s n
LSeries.term_neg_apply.description: This theorem shows that the term for the negation of a sequence at a complex point and a specific index is equal to the negation of the term for the original sequence at that point and index.

LSeries.term_sub.code: LSeries.term_sub (f g : ℕ → ℂ) (s : ℂ) : term (f - g) s = term f s - term g s
LSeries.term_sub.description: This theorem asserts that the nth term of the difference between two sequences at a complex point equals the difference of the nth terms of each sequence at that point.

LSeries.term_sub_apply.code: LSeries.term_sub_apply (f g : ℕ → ℂ) (s : ℂ) (n : ℕ) : term (f - g) s n = term f s n - term g s n
LSeries.term_sub_apply.description: This theorem states that the nth term of the difference between two sequences at a complex point is equal to the difference of the nth terms of each sequence at that point.

LSeries.term_smul.code: LSeries.term_smul (f : ℕ → ℂ) (c s : ℂ) : term (c • f) s = c • term f s
LSeries.term_smul.description: This theorem states that the term of a sequence scaled by a complex constant at a specific point is equal to the scaling of the term of the original sequence at that point by the same constant.

LSeriesSummable.smul.code: LSeriesSummable.smul {f : ℕ → ℂ} (c : ℂ) {s : ℂ} (hf : LSeriesSummable f s) : LSeriesSummable (c • f) s
LSeriesSummable.smul.description: This theorem asserts that scaling a summable sequence by a complex constant preserves its summability at the same complex point.

LSeriesSummable.of_smul.code: LSeriesSummable.of_smul {f : ℕ → ℂ} {c s : ℂ} (hc : c ≠ 0) (hf : LSeriesSummable (c • f) s) : LSeriesSummable f s
LSeriesSummable.of_smul.description: This theorem states that if a sequence scaled by a non-zero complex constant is summable at a complex point, then the original sequence is also summable at that point.

LSeries.term_smul_apply.code: LSeries.term_smul_apply (f : ℕ → ℂ) (c s : ℂ) (n : ℕ) : term (c • f) s n = c * term f s n
LSeries.term_smul_apply.description: This theorem asserts that the nth term of a scalar multiple of a sequence at a complex point is equal to the scalar multiplied by the nth term of the sequence at that point.

LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv.comment:
The abscissa `x : EReal` of absolute convergence of the L-series associated to `f`:
the series converges absolutely at `s` when `re s > x` and does not converge absolutely
when `re s < x`.

explanatories.EReal: This definition introduces a type that represents the extended real numbers, which include negative infinity and positive infinity.
explanatories.InfSet.sInf: A function that computes the infimum of a given set within a framework of ordered structures.
explanatories.Real.toEReal: This defines a function that provides a natural way to include real numbers into the type of extended real numbers.
explanatories.LSeriesSummable: This definition indicates that a sequence is considered L-series summable at a complex point if its L-series converges absolutely at that point.

LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv.fullDefinition: noncomputable def LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv (f : ℕ → ℂ) : EReal :=   sInf <| Real.toEReal '' {x : ℝ | LSeriesSummable f x}
LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv.description: This definition specifies the abscissa of absolute convergence for the L-series associated with a sequence, indicating that the series converges absolutely for complex numbers with a real part greater than this abscissa and does not converge absolutely for real parts less than this abscissa.

LSeriesSummable_of_abscissaOfAbsConv_lt_.code: LSeriesSummable_of_abscissaOfAbsConv_lt_re {f : ℕ → ℂ} {s : ℂ} (hs : abscissaOfAbsConv f < ↑s.re) : LSeriesSummable f s

explanatories.LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv: This definition specifies the abscissa of absolute convergence for the L-series associated with a sequence, indicating that the series converges absolutely for complex numbers with a real part greater than this abscissa and does not converge absolutely for real parts less than this abscissa.

LSeriesSummable_of_abscissaOfAbsConv_lt_.description: If the abscissa of absolute convergence for a sequence is less than the real part of a complex number, then the L-series associated with that sequence converges absolutely at that complex number.

LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv_le_of_forall_l.code:
LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv_le_of_forall_lt_LSeriesSummable {f : ℕ → ℂ} {x : ℝ}
  (h : ∀ (y : ℝ), x < y → LSeriesSummable f ↑y) : abscissaOfAbsConv f ≤ ↑x
LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv_le_of_forall_l.description: If a sequence is L-series summable for all real numbers greater than a certain value, then the abscissa of absolute convergence for that sequence is less than or equal to that value.

LSeriesSummable.abscissaOfAbsConv_le.code: LSeriesSummable.abscissaOfAbsConv_le {f : ℕ → ℂ} {s : ℂ} (h : LSeriesSummable f s) : abscissaOfAbsConv f ≤ ↑s.re

explanatories.LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv: This definition specifies the abscissa of absolute convergence for the L-series associated with a sequence, indicating that the series converges absolutely for complex numbers with a real part greater than this abscissa and does not converge absolutely for real parts less than this abscissa.
explanatories.Complex.re: This defines a function that extracts the real component from a complex number.

LSeriesSummable.abscissaOfAbsConv_le.description: If a sequence is L-series summable at a complex number, then the abscissa of absolute convergence for that sequence is less than or equal to the real part of that complex number.

LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv_le_of_le_const.code:
LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv_le_of_le_const_mul_rpow {f : ℕ → ℂ} {x : ℝ} (h : ∃ C, ∀ (n : ℕ), n ≠ 0 → ‖f n‖ ≤ C * ↑n ^ x) :
  abscissaOfAbsConv f ≤ ↑x + 1
LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv_le_of_le_const.comment:
If `‖f n‖` is bounded by a constant times `n^x`, then the abscissa of absolute convergence
of `f` is bounded by `x + 1`.
LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv_le_of_le_const.description: If the absolute values of the terms in a sequence are bounded above by a constant multiplied by a power of their indices, then the abscissa of absolute convergence for that sequence is less than or equal to one more than the exponent.

LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv_le_of_isBigO_r.code:
LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv_le_of_isBigO_rpow {f : ℕ → ℂ} {x : ℝ} (h : f =O[atTop] fun n => ↑n ^ x) :
  abscissaOfAbsConv f ≤ ↑x + 1
LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv_le_of_isBigO_r.comment:
If `‖f n‖` is `O(n^x)`, then the abscissa of absolute convergence
of `f` is bounded by `x + 1`.

explanatories.Filter.atTop: This definition introduces a filter that captures the behavior of elements approaching infinity in an ordered set, generated by all sets containing elements greater than or equal to any given element.

LSeries.abscissaOfAbsConv_le_of_isBigO_r.description: If a sequence is asymptotically bounded above by a power of the index, then its abscissa of absolute convergence is no greater than one more than the exponent of that power.

toArithmeticFunction.code: toArithmeticFunction.{u_1} {R : Type u_1} [Zero R] (f : ℕ → R) : ArithmeticFunction R
toArithmeticFunction.comment:
We turn any function `ℕ → R` into an `ArithmeticFunction R` by setting its value at `0`
to be zero.

explanatories.rfl: An element is equal to itself, with an implicit argument allowing for broader applications of this concept.

toArithmeticFunction.fullDefinition: def toArithmeticFunction {R : Type*} [Zero R] (f : ℕ → R) : ArithmeticFunction R where   toFun n := if n = 0 then 0 else f n   map_zero' := rfl
toArithmeticFunction.description: This definition specifies a method for converting any function from natural numbers to a ring by assigning its value at zero to be zero so that it qualifies as an arithmetic function.

explanatories.ArithmeticFunction: An arithmetic function is defined as a function from the natural numbers that maps zero to zero, and its multiplication is performed using Dirichlet convolution.

LSeries.convolution.code: LSeries.convolution.{u_1} {R : Type u_1} [Semiring R] (f g : ℕ → R) : ℕ → R
LSeries.convolution.comment:
Dirichlet convolution of two sequences.

We define this in terms of the already existing definition for arithmetic functions.

explanatories.toArithmeticFunction: This definition specifies a method for converting any function from natural numbers to a ring by assigning its value at zero to be zero so that it qualifies as an arithmetic function.

LSeries.convolution.fullDefinition: noncomputable def LSeries.convolution {R : Type*} [Semiring R] (f g : ℕ → R) : ℕ → R :=   ⇑(toArithmeticFunction f * toArithmeticFunction g)
LSeries.convolution.description: This definition describes the Dirichlet convolution operation for two sequences defined on natural numbers within a semiring.

toArithmeticFunction_congr.code:
toArithmeticFunction_congr.{u_1} {R : Type u_1} [Zero R] {f f' : ℕ → R} (h : ∀ {n : ℕ}, n ≠ 0 → f n = f' n) :
  toArithmeticFunction f = toArithmeticFunction f'
toArithmeticFunction_congr.description: This theorem states that if two functions from natural numbers agree on all inputs except zero, then their corresponding arithmetic functions are equal.

ArithmeticFunction.toArithmeticFunction_.code:
ArithmeticFunction.toArithmeticFunction_eq_self.{u_1} {R : Type u_1} [Zero R] (f : ArithmeticFunction R) :
  toArithmeticFunction ⇑f = f
ArithmeticFunction.toArithmeticFunction_.comment:
If we consider an arithmetic function just as a function and turn it back into an
arithmetic function, it is the same as before.
ArithmeticFunction.toArithmeticFunction_.description: This theorem states that applying the conversion process on an arithmetic function to treat it merely as a function results in the original arithmetic function being unchanged.

LSeries.convolution_def.code:
LSeries.convolution_def.{u_1} {R : Type u_1} [Semiring R] (f g : ℕ → R) :
  f ⍟ g = fun n => ∑ p ∈ n.divisorsAntidiagonal, f p.1 * g p.2

explanatories.Nat.divisorsAntidiagonal: The definition states that the antidiagonal divisors of a natural number consist of pairs of natural numbers whose product equals that number, with the special case that zero has no such pairs.

LSeries.convolution_def.description: This theorem defines the convolution of two functions from natural numbers as a sum over the pairs of their divisors, capturing a fundamental operation in number theory.

LSeries.term_convolution.code:
LSeries.term_convolution (f g : ℕ → ℂ) (s : ℂ) (n : ℕ) :
  term (f ⍟ g) s n = ∑ p ∈ n.divisorsAntidiagonal, term f s p.1 * term g s p.2
LSeries.term_convolution.comment:
We give an expression of the `LSeries.term` of the convolution of two functions
in terms of a sum over `Nat.divisorsAntidiagonal`.

LSeries.term_convolution'.code:
LSeries.term_convolution' (f g : ℕ → ℂ) (s : ℂ) :
  term (f ⍟ g) s = fun n => ∑' (b : ↑((fun p => p.1 * p.2) ⁻¹' {n})), term f s (↑b).1 * term g s (↑b).2
LSeries.term_convolution'.comment:
We give an expression of the `LSeries.term` of the convolution of two functions
in terms of an a priori infinte sum over all pairs `(k, m)` with `k * m = n`
(the set we sum over is infinite when `n = 0`). This is the version needed for the
proof that `L (f ⍟ g) = L f * L g`.

explanatories.Set.indicator_of_mem: The theorem demonstrates that if an element is part of a set, then the value of the indicator function for that element equals the value given by a specified function.
explanatories.Set.mem_Ioi: This theorem asserts that an element is part of the interval consisting of elements strictly greater than a given element in a preorder structure if and only if it is greater than that element.
explanatories.Set.not_mem_Ioo_of_ge: This theorem states that if one element is greater than or equal to another in a preorder structure, then the latter cannot belong to the open interval defined by a pair of elements where the first is less than the second.
explanatories.add_zero: This theorem states that in any additive structure with a zero element, adding zero to any element results in that same element.
explanatories.WeakFEPair.hf_modif_int: This theorem states that a modified function related to a weak finite energy pair is locally integrable over the interval of positive real numbers.
explanatories.WeakFEPair.hf_modif_FE: This theorem states that the modified function associated with a weak finite energy pair evaluated at the reciprocal of a positive real number is equal to the product of a complex root number and another modified function scaled by that positive real number raised to a certain exponent.
explanatories.Asymptotics.IsBigO.congr': This theorem establishes that if two functions are asymptotically equal to each other under a specified filter and the first pair has a known Big O relation, then the second pair also maintains that Big O relationship under the same filter.
explanatories.Filter.eventually_gt_atTop: This theorem asserts that in an ordered set without a maximum element, it is true that eventually all elements will be greater than a specified element as one approaches infinity.
explanatories.Filter.Tendsto.congr': A theorem states that if two functions are eventually equal with respect to one filter and one of them tends to a limit under that filter, then the other function also tends to the same limit under the same filters.

WeakFEPair.toStrongFEPair.fullDefinition: def toStrongFEPair : StrongFEPair E where   hf_int   := P.hf_modif_int   hg_int   := P.symm.hf_modif_int   h_feq    := P.hf_modif_FE   hε       := P.hε   hk       := P.hk   hf₀      := rfl   hg₀      := rfl   hf_top r := by     refine (P.hf_top r).congr' ?_ (by rfl)     filter_upwards [eventually_gt_atTop 1] with x hx     rw [f_modif, Pi.add_apply, indicator_of_mem (mem_Ioi.mpr hx),       indicator_of_not_mem (not_mem_Ioo_of_ge hx.le), add_zero, sub_zero]   hg_top r := by     refine (P.hg_top r).congr' ?_ (by rfl)     filter_upwards [eventually_gt_atTop 1] with x hx     rw [f_modif, Pi.add_apply, indicator_of_mem (mem_Ioi.mpr hx),       indicator_of_not_mem (not_mem_Ioo_of_ge hx.le), add_zero, sub_zero]     rfl

HurwitzZeta.hurwitzOddFEPair.fullDefinition: def hurwitzOddFEPair (a : UnitAddCircle) : StrongFEPair ℂ where   f := ofReal' ∘ oddKernel a   g := ofReal' ∘ sinKernel a   hf_int := (continuous_ofReal.comp_continuousOn (continuousOn_oddKernel a)).locallyIntegrableOn     measurableSet_Ioi   hg_int := (continuous_ofReal.comp_continuousOn (continuousOn_sinKernel a)).locallyIntegrableOn     measurableSet_Ioi   k := 3 / 2   hk := by norm_num   hε := one_ne_zero   f₀ := 0   hf₀ := rfl   g₀ := 0   hg₀ := rfl   hf_top r := by     let ⟨v, hv, hv'⟩ := isBigO_atTop_oddKernel a     rw [← isBigO_norm_left] at hv' ⊢     simp_rw [Function.comp_def, sub_zero, norm_real]     exact hv'.trans (isLittleO_exp_neg_mul_rpow_atTop hv _).isBigO   hg_top r := by     let ⟨v, hv, hv'⟩ := isBigO_atTop_sinKernel a     rw [← isBigO_norm_left] at hv' ⊢     simp_rw [Function.comp_def, sub_zero, norm_real]     exact hv'.trans (isLittleO_exp_neg_mul_rpow_atTop hv _).isBigO   h_feq x hx := by simp_rw [Function.comp_apply, one_mul, smul_eq_mul, ← ofReal_mul,     oddKernel_functional_equation a, one_div x, one_div x⁻¹, inv_rpow (le_of_lt hx), one_div,     inv_inv]

HurwitzZeta.evenKernel.fullDefinition: @[irreducible] def evenKernel (a : UnitAddCircle) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=   (show Function.Periodic     (fun ξ : ℝ ↦ rexp (-π * ξ ^ 2 * x) * re (jacobiTheta₂ (ξ * I * x) (I * x))) 1 by       intro ξ       simp only [ofReal_add, ofReal_one, add_mul, one_mul, jacobiTheta₂_add_left']       have : cexp (-↑π * I * ((I * ↑x) + 2 * (↑ξ * I * ↑x))) = rexp (π * (x + 2 * ξ * x)) := by         ring_nf         simp only [I_sq, mul_neg, mul_one, neg_mul, neg_neg, sub_neg_eq_add, ofReal_exp, ofReal_add,           ofReal_mul, ofReal_ofNat]       rw [this, re_ofReal_mul, ← mul_assoc, ← Real.exp_add]       congr       ring).lift a
HurwitzZeta.evenKernel.description: This definition introduces a function that computes the even part of the completed Hurwitz zeta function, specifically represented through its Mellin transform.

HurwitzZeta.hurwitzEvenFEPair.fullDefinition: def hurwitzEvenFEPair (a : UnitAddCircle) : WeakFEPair ℂ where   f := ofReal' ∘ evenKernel a   g := ofReal' ∘ cosKernel a   hf_int := (continuous_ofReal.comp_continuousOn (continuousOn_evenKernel a)).locallyIntegrableOn     measurableSet_Ioi   hg_int := (continuous_ofReal.comp_continuousOn (continuousOn_cosKernel a)).locallyIntegrableOn     measurableSet_Ioi   hk := one_half_pos   hε := one_ne_zero   f₀ := if a = 0 then 1 else 0   hf_top r := by     let ⟨v, hv, hv'⟩ := isBigO_atTop_evenKernel_sub a     rw [← isBigO_norm_left] at hv' ⊢     conv at hv' =>       enter [2, x]; rw [← norm_real, ofReal_sub, apply_ite ((↑) : ℝ → ℂ), ofReal_one, ofReal_zero]     exact hv'.trans (isLittleO_exp_neg_mul_rpow_atTop hv _).isBigO   g₀ := 1   hg_top r := by     obtain ⟨p, hp, hp'⟩ := isBigO_atTop_cosKernel_sub a     rw [← isBigO_norm_left] at hp' ⊢     have (x : ℝ) : ‖(ofReal' ∘ cosKernel a) x - 1‖ = ‖cosKernel a x - 1‖ := by       rw [← norm_real, ofReal_sub, ofReal_one, Function.comp_apply]     simp only [this]     exact hp'.trans (isLittleO_exp_neg_mul_rpow_atTop hp _).isBigO   h_feq x hx := by     simp_rw [Function.comp_apply, one_mul, smul_eq_mul, ← ofReal_mul,       evenKernel_functional_equation, one_div x, one_div x⁻¹, inv_rpow (le_of_lt hx),       one_div, inv_inv]

zeta_eq_tsum_one_div_nat_cpow.code: zeta_eq_tsum_one_div_nat_cpow {s : ℂ} (hs : 1 < s.re) : riemannZeta s = ∑' (n : ℕ), 1 / ↑n ^ s
zeta_eq_tsum_one_div_nat_cpow.comment:
The Riemann zeta function agrees with the naive Dirichlet-series definition when the latter
converges. (Note that this is false without the assumption: when `re s ≤ 1` the sum is divergent,
and we use a different definition to obtain the analytic continuation to all `s`.)

explanatories.riemannZeta: This definition introduces the Riemann zeta function, a complex function important in number theory and related fields.

zeta_eq_tsum_one_div_nat_cpow.description: This theorem establishes that the Riemann zeta function can be expressed as an infinite series of the reciprocals of natural numbers raised to a complex power for values where the real part is greater than one.

zeta_eq_tsum_one_div_nat_add_one_cpow.code: zeta_eq_tsum_one_div_nat_add_one_cpow {s : ℂ} (hs : 1 < s.re) : riemannZeta s = ∑' (n : ℕ), 1 / (↑n + 1) ^ s
zeta_eq_tsum_one_div_nat_add_one_cpow.comment:
Alternate formulation of `zeta_eq_tsum_one_div_nat_cpow` with a `+ 1` (to avoid relying
on mathlib's conventions for `0 ^ s`).

explanatories.riemannZeta: This definition introduces the Riemann zeta function, a complex function important in number theory and related fields.

zeta_eq_tsum_one_div_nat_add_one_cpow.description: This theorem demonstrates that the Riemann zeta function at values greater than one is equivalent to the infinite sum of the reciprocals of natural numbers incremented by one, each raised to the power of the input.

zeta_nat_eq_tsum_of_gt_one.code: zeta_nat_eq_tsum_of_gt_one {k : ℕ} (hk : 1 < k) : riemannZeta ↑k = ∑' (n : ℕ), 1 / ↑n ^ k
zeta_nat_eq_tsum_of_gt_one.comment:
Special case of `zeta_eq_tsum_one_div_nat_cpow` when the argument is in `ℕ`, so the power
function can be expressed using naïve `pow` rather than `cpow`.

zeta_nat_eq_tsum_of_gt_one.description: This theorem shows that the Riemann zeta function evaluated at a natural number greater than one can be represented as an infinite series of the reciprocals of natural numbers raised to that power.

HurwitzZeta.sinZeta_two_mul_nat_add_one.code:
HurwitzZeta.sinZeta_two_mul_nat_add_one {k : ℕ} {x : ℝ} (hk : k ≠ 0) (hx : x ∈ Icc 0 1) :
  sinZeta (↑x) (2 * ↑k + 1) =
    (-1) ^ (k + 1) * (2 * ↑π) ^ (2 * k + 1) / 2 / ↑(2 * k + 1)! *
      Polynomial.eval (↑x) (Polynomial.map (algebraMap ℚ ℂ) (Polynomial.bernoulli (2 * k + 1)))
HurwitzZeta.sinZeta_two_mul_nat_add_one.comment:
Express the value of `sinZeta` at an odd integer `> 1` as a value of the Bernoulli polynomial.

Note that this formula is also correct for `k = 0` (i.e. for the value at `s = 1`), but we do not
prove it in this case, owing to the additional difficulty of working with series that are only
conditionally convergent.
